description: Lake Effect is tackling Be an Earth System Trend Detective, using NASA satellite data to track 20+ years of algal blooms in Lake Erie, right in Windsor’s backyard. I’m Salma, a designer and brand builder leading design, storytelling and our pitch. We have a clear plan and a polished identity ready. Looking for: a Python/data person, a web developer for an interactive map, and an Earth science enthusiast. All levels welcome. Let’s make some waves! 🌊
summary:
Lake Effect is a website that shows which environmental changes in a lake are real. Built for NASA's "Be an Earth System Trend Detective" challenge, it answers the challenge's four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and is the change significant? Pick one of the five Great Lakes and our Trend Scanner tests every variable with a Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope, ranks them by real change, and maps where the change happens, pixel by pixel. A change only counts when it is statistically significant (p < 0.05), so the tool separates real signals from year-to-year noise.

This matters because harmful algal blooms return to Lake Erie every summer, typically July to October (NOAA), and reach the beaches and drinking water of our own city, Windsor. NASA MODIS-Aqua satellite data shows algae in Lake Erie rising about 1.55 mg/m³ per decade from 2003 to 2025, a significant trend (p < 0.001) across most of the lake. Bloom-season water temperature drifted up about 0.41 °C per decade, but that is not significant yet, and our tool says so instead of overclaiming.
details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?

Lake Effect helps anyone see which environmental changes in a lake are real. Instead of drawing a trend line and hoping, it tests every variable for statistical significance, ranks them from the strongest real change to none, and shows where in the lake the change is happening.

1. Data: we download satellite data for the five Great Lakes: NASA MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll-a (a measure of algae, about 4 km pixels, 2003–2025) and NOAA GLSEA lake surface temperature (about 1.4 km pixels, 2007–2025). We cut the data to each lake's shoreline.

2. Bloom season: we average each variable over July to October, NOAA's typical Lake Erie bloom season, for every year: for the whole lake, a western and an eastern part, and every satellite pixel. In Lake Erie the western basin is west of 82.5° W.

3. Trend Scanner: our Python code runs the Mann-Kendall test on every series and pixel. A change counts as real only when p < 0.05, and Sen's slope gives its size per decade.

4. Website: you pick a lake from a menu and see a ranked list of variables, maps of algae and water temperature with a slider to move through the years (algae 2003–2025, temperature 2007–2025), a map of where the long-term change is significant, a chart over time for each part of the lake, and a guided story for Lake Erie.

What benefits does it have?

It answers the challenge's hardest question, "is it significant?", clearly and honestly. It shows that Lake Erie's summer water temperature has drifted upward but is not yet a significant trend, instead of overclaiming. It also shows exactly where change happens: in Lake Erie, algae is rising significantly in 1,300 of 1,593 satellite pixels, in both the western basin (+1.34 mg/m³ per decade) and the central and eastern basins (+1.39), and no pixel shows a significant decrease. Water temperature also gets a basin-level check: in the western basin, where most blooms happen, it drifted up 0.46 °C per decade, but that is not significant yet (p = 0.11). The result holds when we drop the two highest recent years and when we correct the test for autocorrelation. Anyone can use it in a web browser, for free, with no login and no software to install.

What is the intended impact?

We want residents, students and local decision-makers to understand their own lake with real numbers instead of guesses. In Windsor-Essex, algal blooms affect drinking water, public health, beaches and tourism (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit; Essex Region Conservation Authority). A simple, honest trend detector can show which changes are worth acting on and where to look first. Because the same tool already runs on all five Great Lakes, communities across the region can use it, and it can be extended to any lake with satellite data.

What tools did you use?

Data: NASA MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll-a (NASA Ocean Biology DAAC, found with Earthdata Search and downloaded with an Earthdata Login) and NOAA GLERL GLSEA lake surface temperature (GLERL ERDDAP).

Analysis: Python with pandas, NumPy, xarray, netCDF4, geopandas, shapely and pymannkendall.

Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet (maps), Chart.js (charts) and OpenStreetMap (background map), hosted free on GitHub Pages. Code and teamwork: GitHub.

AI assistants: Claude, ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot (see "Use of AI" below).

How is your project creative?

Most trend tools draw a line and let you guess. Lake Effect tests every variable and every satellite pixel, ranks variables by how much they really changed, and is open about results that are not significant yet. Instead of one number for a whole lake, it maps significance pixel by pixel, so you can see where change is real. It starts from a local story, algae on Windsor's beaches, and then scales the same method to all five Great Lakes with one menu.

What factors did your team consider?

Cost: everything is free. NASA and NOAA data are open, every library is open source, and the site is hosted free on GitHub Pages. When a map service started asking for a paid key, we switched to free options.

Time: we had one weekend, so we focused on two variables and told the Lake Erie story first. Precipitation (NASA MERRA-2) is a next step.

Scientific honesty: we chose the bloom season from NOAA before looking at results, so we couldn't pick the months that look best. In Lake Erie we kept only pixels with at least 15 years of data and checked our main result in two other ways. Satellite chlorophyll shows how much algae there is, not how toxic it is, and our trends show change, not causes. For lakes other than Erie, the western and eastern sections split each lake at its middle.

Access: the site loads fast (we shrank the map data from 187 MB to 17 MB), works on phones and laptops, and needs no login.

Use of AI

We used AI assistants as tools, as allowed by the rules. The project idea came from our team: Salma lives in Windsor, where algal blooms affect local beaches. Claude (Anthropic) helped plan the work and write most of the starter code (the Trend Scanner and the website), documents, slides and graphics. ChatGPT (OpenAI) helped our data lead write the data download and processing scripts and the five-lakes maps. GitHub Copilot helped with the website's error handling and the map year slider. Our team chose the science from cited sources, downloaded and processed the data, ran the analysis and reviewed every result. AI-assisted code is marked at the top of each file and in the README, the website footer credits the AI tools, and AI-generated images carry a visible "AI-generated" label (the deck cover graphic).
